national_monitoring_scale.source: Bangladesh Water Development Board (BWDB), national river/basin inventory (bwdb.gov.bd), retrieved 2026
national_monitoring_scale.note: The 405-entry BWDB list and DoE's own monitoring-network list are compiled for different purposes (basin/flow inventory vs. water-quality lab sampling) and are not a perfectly like-for-like match, but the order of magnitude is a fair, citable illustration of why an inspection-priority tool matters: Bangladesh's own environmental regulator can put monthly lab sampling on only a small fraction of the country's named rivers.

coastal_salinity_climate_context.source: Climate Change Cell, Department of Environment (2016), 'Assessment of Sea Level Rise on Bangladesh Coast through Trend Analysis' -- 30-year tidal record (BWDB/BIWTA gauges), Sen's slope + Mann-Kendall significance testing at 95% confidence.
coastal_salinity_climate_context.relevance_to_aquasentinel_rivers: Pashur, Rupsha, and Kakshiali -- three of the rivers in AquaSentinel's merged Bangladesh dataset with the most extreme observed salinity/chloride -- sit in the Ganges Tidal Floodplain (Western Coastal Region), the zone this DoE study measured at 7-8 mm/year sea-level rise. DoE's own River Water Quality Report 2015 recorded chloride up to 12,692 mg/l (Pashur), 10,082 mg/l (Rupsha) and 13,124 mg/l (Kakshiali) against an EQS limit of 600 mg/l.
coastal_salinity_climate_context.caveat: This is documented regional climate context from an independent DoE study, presented alongside the salinity readings -- it is NOT a new regression or causal estimate fitted by AquaSentinel; the available salinity time series for these rivers (2015 monthly + sparse 2021-2023 averages) is too short to responsibly fit its own trend line.
